name: correct-svg

version.labels: L1 2026-11-08 per-depth kinds, acceptable kinds and sketches, written before any run

measures: Does the author write correct diagram JSON at each depth (overview: plain-word labels, no formulas, simplest kind; standard: the mechanism with its terms; deep: the formula or exact relationship in labels, a plot or chart when a quantity is involved, maths in $...$). Run with --depths overview,standard,deep.
written: 2026-11-08, before any correct-svg card was sent
notation: Per depth: kinds = right diagram kinds (a picture or a second diagram beside it is allowed), acceptableKinds = weaker kinds; sketch = what the nodes, axes and edges must say. best/acceptable mixes are derived from these per depth.

prompts.prompt: how does the water cycle work?

sketch: Steps in plain words: water evaporates from the sea, forms clouds, falls as rain or snow, flows back to the sea.
The arrows close the loop back to the start; no formulas or technical terms.
Evaporation -> condensation -> precipitation -> collection (runoff, groundwater), back to evaporation.
The sun's heat drives evaporation; cooling air drives condensation.
The loop with exact terms: evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, infiltration, runoff.
Labels may carry quantities (solar energy in, latent heat released on condensation); still a closed cycle.

prompts.prompt: how does the TCP handshake work?

sketch: Two actors, your computer and the server, exchange three messages: hello, hello back, OK.
Plain words, in order; no flag names.
Client -> server SYN; server -> client SYN-ACK; client -> server ACK; then the connection is open.
Each message labelled with its flag name.
Client -> server SYN seq=x; server -> client SYN-ACK seq=y, ack=x+1; client -> server ACK ack=y+1.
Sequence and acknowledgement numbers in the labels show what each side confirms.
Layers from the ground up in plain words: where weather happens, where planes fly and the ozone sits, where meteors burn up, where satellites orbit.
Bottom to top; numbers not needed.
Troposphere, stratosphere (ozone layer), mesosphere, thermosphere, exosphere, bottom to top.
One fact per layer: weather, ozone absorbs UV, meteors burn up, aurora and the ISS.
The five layers with heights: troposphere 0-12 km, stratosphere 12-50 km, mesosphere 50-85 km, thermosphere 85-600 km, exosphere above.
The temperature trend of each layer (falls, rises, falls, rises) in its label or detail.

prompts.prompt: how does a binary search tree work?

sketch: A small tree of numbers: smaller numbers go left, bigger numbers go right.
Plain words; one root at the top.
A binary tree of keys where each left subtree is smaller and each right subtree larger (e.g. 8 with 3 and 10; 3 with 1 and 6).
A search compares the key with each node and goes left or right.
A binary-layout tree of keys with the search path for one key shown: left when key < node, right when key > node.
The labels or caption state O(log n) search on a balanced tree and O(n) in the worst case.

prompts.prompt: how did the Roman Empire rise and fall?

sketch: A few big moments in order: Rome grows, becomes an empire, splits in two, the West falls.
Plain words; rough dates allowed.
27 BC Augustus the first emperor; 117 AD greatest extent; 285 AD split into East and West; 476 AD fall of the West.
Events in time order with their dates.
Dated events: 27 BC Augustus, 117 AD peak under Trajan, 235-284 crisis, 285 Diocletian splits the empire, 410 sack of Rome, 476 last Western emperor deposed, 1453 the East falls.
Each event's detail names its cause or consequence.
Before: things neatly ordered (ice cubes, a sorted deck); after: spread out and mixed (water, a shuffled deck).
Plain words: things tend to spread out on their own; no formula.
Before: low entropy, few possible arrangements; after: high entropy, many arrangements; operation: energy spreads out over time.
Names arrangements (microstates) and the second law: an isolated system's entropy does not decrease.
The formula S = k_B ln W (or Delta S = Q / T) in $...$, with the number of arrangements W before and after.
A bar chart or plot of entropy rising with the number of arrangements, values computed from the formula.
A node where every item is one class (pure) next to a mixed node (impure).
Plain words: the more mixed, the higher the impurity; no formula.
Bars of a node's class shares (e.g. 3 A, 1 B), and how a split makes the children purer.
Terms: impurity, split, class share; the purer child scores lower.
x axis: the share p of one class in a node, 0 to 1; y axis: Gini impurity 1 - (p^2 + (1-p)^2) = 2p(1-p): 0 at p = 0 and 1, peak 0.5 at p = 0.5.
Or bars of one node's class shares, with the impurity 1 - (sum of squared shares) stated and computed from those bars.
The true answer next to the model's guess: a confident right guess costs little, a confident wrong guess costs a lot.
Plain words; no logarithms.
Bars of the true distribution (one-hot) and the predicted probabilities; the loss is high when the true class gets a low probability.
Terms: predicted probability, true label, loss.
x axis: predicted probability of the true class, 0 to 1; y axis: loss -ln(p), very large near 0 and 0 at p = 1.
Or bars of the true distribution next to the predicted one, with H(p, q) = -sum p log q computed from the bar values.
Before: raw scores; after: shares that add up to 100%, the biggest score keeping the biggest share.
Plain words; no exponentials.
Before: logits (e.g. 2.0, 1.0, 0.1); after: probabilities about 0.66, 0.24, 0.10; operation: exponentiate, then divide by the sum.
Terms: logits, probabilities, normalise.
Before: raw scores (logits) such as 2.0, 1.0, 0.1; after: probabilities e^z_i / sum_j e^z_j, about 0.66, 0.24, 0.10.
The outputs are all positive and sum to 1; the largest score keeps the largest share.

prompts.prompt: what does the sigmoid activation function do?

sketch: Any input number is squashed into the range 0 to 1: a big negative input gives nearly 0, a big positive input nearly 1.
Plain words; no formula.
An S-shaped curve: input z on the x axis, output between 0 and 1 on the y axis, 0.5 at z = 0.
Terms: activation, saturation, probability-like output.
x axis: input z, about -6 to 6; y axis: sigmoid(z) = 1 / (1 + e^-z), an S-curve from 0 to 1.
It passes 0.5 at z = 0 and flattens near 0 and 1 (saturation).

prompts.prompt: what is a learning rate schedule?

sketch: Big steps early in training, smaller steps later.
Plain words: the learning rate goes down over time.
The learning rate on y against the training step on x, falling (step decay or cosine, maybe after a warm-up).
Terms: learning rate, warm-up, decay.
x axis: training step or epoch; y axis: learning rate falling over training (step decay, exponential decay or cosine; a warm-up rising first if named).
The plotted values follow the schedule formula the prose states (for example lr_t = lr_0 * gamma^t).
Walk downhill one step at a time until you reach the bottom.
Plain words: look at the slope, step down, repeat.
A loop: compute the gradient (slope) of the loss -> step against it, scaled by the learning rate -> repeat until the loss stops falling.
Terms: loss, gradient, learning rate.
x axis: a parameter w; y axis: the loss L(w), a bowl; steps move downhill toward the minimum.
Each step is w <- w - eta * dL/dw: the learning rate eta times the slope sets the step size.
Each word looks at the other words and decides how much each one matters to it.
Plain words: the most relevant words get the most attention.
The query compared with every key gives scores; softmax turns them into weights that sum to 1; the weights mix the values.
Terms: query, key, value, weights.
Scores: the query dotted with every key, divided by sqrt(d_k); softmax turns one query's scores into weights that sum to 1.
The output is the weighted sum of the value vectors; a larger weight means that token contributes more.

prompts.prompt: what is the difference between precision and recall?

sketch: Precision: of the items you flagged, how many were right; recall: of the right items, how many you found.
Plain words; an example with counts allowed, no formulas.
Confusion counts with example numbers: true positives, false positives, false negatives, true negatives.
Precision uses TP and FP; recall uses TP and FN.
Confusion counts with example numbers: true positives, false positives, false negatives (and true negatives).
Precision = TP / (TP + FP) and recall = TP / (TP + FN), each computed from those same counts.
